meta.title: Who really said "Everything we hear is an opinion, not a fact. Everything we see is a perspective, not the truth"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Marcus Aurelius never wrote this. It is a modern paraphrase that loosely echoes Meditations 2.15 (“all is opinion”) but appears in none of his works.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Everything we hear is an opinion, not a fact. Everything we see is a perspective, not the truth'?
meta.ogDescription: PolitiFact, Check Your Fact & Wikiquote agree: Marcus Aurelius never wrote this line. It's a modern paraphrase loosely riffing on Meditations 2.15.

answer.label: Not Marcus Aurelius — a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording appears in none of Marcus Aurelius’s writings. Fact-checkers and Stoic scholars trace it to a modern paraphrase that loosely echoes Meditations 2.15 (“all is but opinion”) — but the seed thought is stretched into a subjective relativism Marcus, a Stoic rather than a skeptic, would not have endorsed. Historian and Marcus Aurelius biographer Donald Robertson bluntly calls it “a fake quote”.

source.heading: Where this line really comes from

source.excerpt: Everything we hear is an opinion, not a fact. Everything we see is a perspective, not the truth.
trail: PolitiFact rated the attribution “False”, quoting philosopher Dirk Baltzly — who called the wording “just vaguely possible” as a creative translation but concluded “I’d call BS on that quote.”
Check Your Fact found no occurrence in his works; biographer Donald Robertson said “That’s a fake quote” and Daily Stoic author Stephen Hanselman called it a loose paraphrase.
Wikiquote editors trace the wording to a paraphrasing website, noting it renders only three Greek words (“all is opinion”) from 2.15, with related ideas at 12.8, 12.22 and 12.26.
Modern Stoicism shows the paraphrase reverses Marcus’s meaning: he held reason can objectively judge, not that all perspectives are equally valid.
source.excerptNote: The genuine line it distantly echoes is Meditations 2.15: “Remember that all is but opinion and conceit, for those things are plain and apparent, which were spoken unto Monimus the Cynic.” Marcus’s point was that our judgements about things, not the things themselves, disturb us — not that facts and truth do not exist.

sourceLink.text: PolitiFact: No, Marcus Aurelius didn’t say this

source.rightsNote: The exact wording is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identifiable author, publication, or date, so no copyright status can be asserted for it. The genuine passage it echoes — Meditations 2.15 — is ancient and long in the public domain, and the Casaubon (1634) and 19th-century English translations shown here are also public domain; but that says nothing about the modern paraphrase itself.

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.heading: Who was Marcus Aurelius?
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius (121–180 AD) was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and the last of the “Five Good Emperors.” His private notebook, the Meditations, written in Greek during his military campaigns, is a foundational text of Stoic philosophy. Because he is a byword for calm wisdom, he is one of the internet’s most magnetic targets for feel-good quotes he never wrote — this line among them.

misattribution.heading: A paraphrase mistaken for the man
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet-name” misattribution: a modern, share-friendly line pinned on antiquity’s most quotable Stoic. The words are not in the Meditations or anywhere else in his writings.

items.why: The exact sentence appears in none of his works. Wikiquote traces it to a paraphrasing website that inflated three Greek words of Meditations 2.15 into two full sentences.

The paraphrase reads as subjective relativism — every perspective equally valid. But Marcus was a Stoic, not a skeptic: as Modern Stoicism explains, he held that reason can objectively judge, and that facts exist but should not disturb us.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine seed is Meditations 2.15 — “Remember that all is but opinion” — which is about mastering our judgements, not about denying that truth exists (Casaubon translation, Gutenberg).

context.heading: Why the distinction matters
lead: The paraphrase is popular precisely because it sounds like liberating wisdom: nothing you’re told is fact, nothing you see is truth. But that is closer to the modern slogan “there are no facts, only interpretations” (a line associated with Nietzsche’s notebooks) than to Stoicism.

Marcus’s actual teaching runs the other way: external things are real, but our opinions about them are what cause distress — so we should discipline the judgement, not dissolve the facts. Flattening his Stoicism into “everything is just perspective” loses the whole point of the Meditations.
detailsBody: Meditations 2.15 (Casaubon, 1634): “Remember that all is but opinion and conceit, for those things are plain and apparent, which were spoken unto Monimus the Cynic.”

Related judgement-focused passages the fact-checkers cite include 4.7 (“Do away with the judgement, and the notion ‘I have been harmed’ is done away with”) and Wikiquote’s pointers to 12.8, 12.22 and 12.26.
context.pull: “Remember that all is but opinion” — about judgement, not the denial of truth.
